findings.title: Swift round-trip drops pose and racket ownership
findings.why_it_matters: A desktop-generated portable package loses every player's pose keypoints and each racket's player_id after iOS imports and re-exports it. The iOS importer decodes frames into these narrower Codable structs, stores that decoded representation, and AnalysisStore.export serializes it again, so the loss is permanent and downstream desktop review can no longer render the original pose data or retain racket ownership. Representing both optional fields in the Swift frame types preserves the established v1 frame contract while remaining compatible with iOS-produced records that omit them.

findings.title: Incomplete imports are silently marked complete
findings.why_it_matters: An analysis folder missing frames, events, or corrections is accepted, and the new store is then marked complete. A damaged transfer can therefore appear successfully imported while silently losing predictions or durable human edits; the Start/Continue action also returns immediately because the store says complete. Requiring the declared artifacts and preserving the manifest status prevents corrupt or paused packages from being converted into false completions.

findings.title: Point-event clip export always rejects
findings.why_it_matters: Users cannot export clips for hits or bounces from the desktop event UI: the shared event contract requires point events to have end equal to start, while this handler forwards that zero-length interval to an exporter that requires start to be strictly less than end. Every normal hit/bounce reaches the same deterministic error. Expanding point events to a bounded interval around the timestamp, as the iOS ClipExporter already does, makes the advertised event export usable while preserving rally intervals.

findings.title: Completion is committed before portable export succeeds
findings.why_it_matters: A native analysis can be recorded as complete even when writing frames.jsonl, events.json, corrections.json, or manifest.json fails. On the next attempt, the early complete-status return skips both analysis and export, so the user is left with stale or empty interoperable artifacts and no automatic recovery path. Exporting first and committing complete only after all artifacts succeed keeps the resumable database status aligned with the package users can actually open.

findings.title: Package import blocks the main actor
findings.why_it_matters: Importing a large analysis folder can freeze the entire interface while it copies the source video, hashes it, decodes every JSONL frame, and populates SQLite. The import is invoked synchronously from a SwiftUI task, so the progress overlay cannot remain responsive and a multi-gigabyte package can be terminated by the watchdog. Move the synchronous package pipeline to a non-main executor and publish only the final state transition on the main actor.

findings.title: Resume decodes every previously completed frame
findings.why_it_matters: Resuming near the end of a long match starts AVAssetReader at the original media origin and decodes the entire completed prefix again, discarding each frame before inference. For the supported two-hour videos, repeated pauses can impose a large and growing restart delay and unnecessary decode energy. Starting the reader near the last committed timestamp while retaining the strict timestamp skip restores only the required GOP prefix and keeps VFR safety.

findings.title: Court corrections are decoded for every frame
findings.why_it_matters: Every analyzed frame performs a SQLite metadata query and JSON-decodes the complete corrections object. A two-hour 30 fps match invokes this path about 216,000 times, and the decoded dictionary grows as calibrations and labels are added. Caching corrections outside the frame loop removes this avoidable database and allocation work from the inference hot path.

findings.title: Failed event saves still dismiss editor
findings.why_it_matters: A SQLite or refresh failure discards the user's in-progress event form because the editor dismisses even though persistence failed. The parent records an alert after swallowing the error, but the edited values are already gone and must be re-entered.
